items.title: Samsung’s Tizen-based Galaxy Watch gets an unofficial Wear OS 3.5 port
items.summary:
TL;DR 

A developer has released an unofficial Wear OS 3.5 port based on Android 11 for the original Samsung Galaxy Watch (SM-R800). 
 The port uses Pixel Watch software and reportedly supports Gemini, the Play Store, GPS, and health tracking. 
 The port and installation guide are available on GitHub, though it remains experimental. 

Samsung’s switch from Tizen to Wear OS in 2021 opened up a whole new world of apps and Google services for Galaxy Watch owners. But you needed a Galaxy Watch 4 or newer to enjoy those benefits. Older models were left behind, and as Samsung wound down its Tizen smartwatch ecosystem , their usefulness gradually diminished. However, one developer is giving the original Galaxy Watch another shot at life.

A developer known as Depth118 has shared an unofficial Android 11-based Wear OS 3.5 port on GitHub for Samsung’s 2018 Galaxy Watch. The project uses software from the original Google Pixel Watch, which, despite launching four years later, shares the same Exynos 9110 processor. The port is specifically designed for the 46mm Bluetooth Galaxy Watch (SM-R800), and the list of features the developer claims to have working is surprisingly extensive.

items.title: Dev behind top PS3 emulator on Android releases ARMFlash, bringing tons of Flash games to Android
items.summary:
Credit: Hadlee Simons / Android Authority 

TL;DR 

A key developer behind the ARMSX2 and ARMSX3 emulators has released ARMFlash on Android. 
 This app is a port of the Flashpoint Archive project and lets you play over 200,000 web-based games and experiences on Android. 
 ARMFlash supports both touch and controller input, while system requirements are very modest. 

We’ve seen a few apps that let you play Flash games on Android in recent times, most notably Swiff. Now, one of the key developers behind the ARMSX2 and ARMSX3 emulators has released ARMFlash.

ARMFlash was released on GitHub yesterday (November 23) by developer jpolo1224, allowing you to play Flash, HTML 5, Shockwave, Java, and PopCap games on Android. ARMFlash is actually a port of the Flashpoint Archive project for PCs, which has saved over 200,000 old web-based games, animations, and interactive experiences.

items.title: The best Android keyboard app isn’t on the Play Store. Here’s how to install it
items.summary:
Credit: Dhruv Bhutani / Android Authority 

Android’s always been the go-to destination when it comes to customisation and dialing in the experience exactly as you want it, and that extends to switching out the keyboard for something a bit more bespoke. For the longest time, finding a good keyboard for Android usually meant choosing between Gboard and SwiftKey . Both are excellent at predicting what you’re going to type, correcting spelling mistakes and letting you swipe between letters. The catch is that both these keyboards are made by mega corps, Google and Microsoft, and data collection is part and parcel of the deal.

That’s why I’ve been looking at HeliBoard. It’s a free, open-source keyboard that offers many of the same features you’d expect from a modern Android keyboard without needing an internet connection, and, most importantly, no data collection. There are no advertisements, no cloud-based processing and plenty of customization options as is to be expected with open-source apps. There’s just one catch, you won’t find the app on the Google Play Store.
items.t: The best Android keyboard app isn’t on the Play Store. Here’s how to install it

items.title: Gemini could soon let you create your own custom voice from scratch
items.summary:
TL;DR 

Google is working on a “Create a voice” feature that could let Gemini users design custom voices using text prompts. 
 Users could describe their preferred accent, tone, speaking speed, and other vocal characteristics instead of choosing from preset voices. 
 The feature could also include a “Surprise me” option for discovering new voices without writing a prompt. 

For all the progress we’ve made with voice assistants over the years, personalizing how they sound still feels a little like picking a ringtone in the early 2000s. You’re given a list of options, listen to a few, and settle for whichever sounds closest to what you want. Even with Google adding 66 new regional voices to Gemini just last week, that’s essentially how things work today. But our latest discovery suggests Google could soon let you play casting director and create a voice of your own.

APK teardown: This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

We’ve discovered new strings in version 17.78.13 of the Google app pointing to a new “Create a voice” option in Gemini’s voice selection menu. Instead of choosing from a collection of voices Google has designed for you, you can describe how you want your assistant to sound using your own words. There’s even a “Surprise me” option that could come up with something for you when you’re short on ideas.
items.t: Gemini could soon let you create your own custom voice from scratch

While digging through the latest version of the Google app (v17.78.13), we spotted several new strings pointing to a sticker-creation experience coming to Gemini. They reveal options to copy stickers, share individual stickers, and even download an entire sticker pack.

items.title: Google gives publishers more visibility in AI Mode with new ‘Dive Deeper’ links
items.summary:
TL;DR 

Google has started rolling out its previously announced “Dive Deeper” section in Search’s AI Mode. 
 The section displays prominent blue links, image thumbnails, and descriptions of related articles below AI-generated responses. 
 The change aims to encourage further exploration of topics while giving publishers more visibility in AI-powered search results. 

Google’s efforts to turn Search into an answer engine have left publishers fighting for clicks and some users missing the depth that traditional search results offered. While AI Mode has made researching topics less time-consuming, Google recognizes that getting a quick answer isn’t always the end of someone’s search journey. To address this, the company is now rolling out a new “Dive Deeper” section in AI Mode to encourage readers to explore articles beyond its AI-generated answers.

SEO consultant Glenn Gabe spotted and shared the change on X (via Search Engine Roundtable ). The section appears at the bottom of AI Mode responses and features prominent blue links, image thumbnails, and descriptions explaining what each article offers. It’s one of several improvements Google announced last month.
items.t: Google gives publishers more visibility in AI Mode with new ‘Dive Deeper’ links

items.title: Motorcyclists spot Google Maps on Android Auto showing routes for two-wheeled vehicles
items.summary:
Credit: KTM 

TL;DR 

Some Android Auto users report that a new motorcycle icon has appeared on Google Maps. 
 The users claim that the app has switched to motorcycle mode. 
 The app is now showing routes meant for two-wheeled vehicles, in addition to car routes. 

It’s pretty common to see reports about bugs on Android Auto. For example, users were recently having trouble with music controls . However, every now and then, you’ll come across reports about something exciting. Fortunately, today falls into the latter category, especially for those who own motorcycles.

Android Auto tends to be a car-centric experience. When using Google Maps on Android Auto, the platform normally defaults to car routes. That is true whether you’re driving in a car or some other type of vehicle. That’s why some users were taken by surprise when Google Maps on Android Auto began showing routes meant for two-wheeled vehicles.
items.t: Motorcyclists spot Google Maps on Android Auto showing routes for two-wheeled vehicles

items.title: Google Chrome is working on 3 new filters to narrow down your browsing history
items.summary:
TL;DR 

Google is working on three new Chrome history filters that let users narrow down browsing activity by device, date, and who browsed. 
 The Who browsed filter separates websites visited by users from those accessed by Gemini. 
 The filters have been spotted in Chrome Dev and Canary, but enabling their experimental flags doesn’t appear to activate them for everyone. 

Google is working on introducing new filters to help you sift through your Chrome history, and these go way more granular than you might have expected. The browser could soon get three new history search filters, and one of them could even let you swap between websites you visited yourself and those that were accessed by Gemini.

The development was spotted and highlighted by X user @Leopeva64 , who even shared screenshots of the redesigned history section with the new filters visible. According to the browser tipster, the new filters are already available in the Dev and Canary versions of Chrome, suggesting that they could likely go stable sometime soon.
items.t: Google Chrome is working on 3 new filters to narrow down your browsing history

Launched globally this fall, the RayNeo GT Max and RayNeo iO pair premium materials and bleeding-edge optics with the one thing Mac and iPhone owners actually want from a display accessory — plug it in, and it works.

RayNeo isn’t a small player making a big claim here. The company took the No. 1 spot in global AR smart glasses shipments across the first half of 2026, with 24.8% market share according to IDC and 23.9% according to Counterpoint Research.

Its Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is live now through November 30, with the flagship GT Max at $335 (down from $429), the lighter GT at $249 (down from $329), and the camera-free iO smart glasses at $389 (down from $499). Everything is available on RayNeo.com and Amazon US.
